brief: A utensil holder with two bins that is waterproof and dishwasher safe.

requirements.requirement: A utensil holder: holds kitchen utensils standing up
requirements.evidence: A fork (prop:1) stands upright in bin:0,0,0 and a spoon (prop:2) in bin:-1,0,0. Both can be seen in the view.
Two full-depth bins: bin:0,0,0~hex-bin-full and bin:-1,0,0~hex-bin-full.

The configurator only checks fit. Whether it's watertight depends on the material and how it's printed, which can't be checked here. The solid-floor bins (no drain holes) are the only part of the shape that helps.
Surviving a dishwasher's heat and detergent depends on the material, and the configurator knows nothing about materials.

finish.summary: I built the utensil holder with two bins, but I can't say it's waterproof or dishwasher safe. It's two full-height hex bases joined side by side and bolted together. Each one holds a full-depth bin with a solid floor (no drain holes). All open faces have end caps. 14 parts, about 1074 g of filament. To show what it's for, a fork stands in one bin and a spoon in the other. A knife wouldn't fit in the space left. The configurator's checks pass and its mesh-collision check reads clear. It only checks fit and collisions, though. Whether the holder keeps water out or survives a dishwasher depends on the plastic and print settings you choose, and nothing here can test that. The solid floors are the only part of the shape that helps hold water.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
